As synthetic text reaches an estimated 20--60\% of web corpora, detect-and-reweight methods that downweight likely-synthetic samples via $w(x) = (1-q(x))^b$ have gained traction.
Two questions remain open: does hard filtering outperform soft reweighting, and how should the exponent $b$ be set without per-model grid search?

Through controlled experiments (Qwen3-0.6B continued pretraining on self-generated contamination, 132M FineWeb tokens, 40\% contamination, 3 seeds), we identify an epoch-exposure confound and investigate distribution matching.
Detect and Remove (D\&R) owes the bulk of its reported advantage to multi-epoch exposure: at matched content epochs, the gap shrinks from 0.393 (D\&R seed\,42) to 0.026 perplexity ($N{=}3$).
Adaptive reweighting yields small but consistent improvements across both in-distribution and out-of-distribution evaluation ($|\Delta| < 0.01$ PPL), with no evidence of distribution matching.
A dual-constrained adaptive $b^*$, selecting the minimum exponent that satisfies a quality floor while preserving gradient stability, improves over uniform training ($\Delta{=}{-}0.010$ PPL) without requiring grid search, though a gap to the grid-optimal setting remains; detector signal type appears to matter more than discrimination accuracy (3 detectors, single seed).
The method fails at $\rho{=}0.2$ and shows no effect at 1.7B; with $N{=}3$, we report effect sizes and directional consistency rather than formal significance.

\subsection{Main Results}
\label{sec:main-results}

Table~\ref{tab:main} reports held-out perplexity at $\rho = 0.4$ across three seeds.
Continued pretraining reduces PPL from 22.970 (pretrained checkpoint) to the 17.3--17.8 range; the initial 5.2-point drop absorbs the bulk of easy gains, and reweighting method comparisons operate within a narrow residual.

Adaptive $\bstar$ achieves 3-seed mean PPL 17.674, compared to 17.694 for uniform ($\Delta{=}{-}0.019$) and 17.620 for grid $b{=}0.3$ (3-seed mean; gap $+$0.054).
The practical value is eliminating $b$ grid search (nine full training runs~\citep{drayson2025detection}, ${\sim}$16 GPU-hours at 0.6B scale), though grid search yields a larger improvement.
The grid-best $b{=}0.3$ is a post-hoc oracle from nine candidates; the noisy PPL plateau at $b \in [0.1, 0.5]$ (Figure~\ref{fig:grid_b_trend}) makes validation-based selection unreliable.
At the nearest fixed point ($b{=}1.0$), PPL equals uniform (17.692 vs.\ 17.694): per-batch adaptation is essential.

The ablation hierarchy at $\rho{=}0.4$ (Adaptive ${<}$ Uniform ${<}$ ESS-only ${<}$ Random, Table~\ref{tab:main}) reveals two requirements for effective reweighting: detector signal and minimum intervention.
Random weights $\mathcal{U}(0,2)$ (17.802) confirm that detector $q$-scores carry genuine provenance signal; uninformed reweighting only increases gradient variance.
ESS-only (mean $17.738 {\pm} 0.022$) uses the same $q$-scores but maximizes $b$ up to the stability ceiling, concentrating weights on a few high-confidence samples; it provides no improvement over uniform.
Only the dual-constrained adaptive method, which limits $b$ to the minimum needed, improves in-distribution PPL over uniform (mean $\Delta{=}{-}0.019$, directionally consistent across all seeds).
Figure~\ref{fig:grid_b_trend} contextualizes this: the grid curve has a broad plateau at $b \in [0.1, 0.5]$ (PPL 17.620--17.655); adaptive $\bstar$ (mean PPL 17.674) improves over uniform but does not reach the plateau, while ESS-only $\bstar$ (mean 3.5--5.9) lies in the degradation zone beyond it.

Golden Ratio~\citep{he2025golden} achieves 17.654 (seed\,42), outperforming adaptive $\bstar$ (mean 17.674, gap 0.020) at the cost of requiring oracle access to the true contamination ratio $\rho$.

\paragraph{Hard filtering and the epoch confound.}
Detect \& Remove at its best threshold ($q{>}0.3$) achieves 3-seed mean PPL $17.250 \pm 0.001$ at full training length, apparently outperforming all reweighting methods by a wide margin.
However, filtering retains only 31.5\% of tokens, so the model sees surviving data ${\sim}$3.2 \emph{content epochs} (times each unique document is seen) versus one for reweighting.
An epoch-matched control (training D\&R at $q{>}0.5$ for 2{,}533 steps to equalize content epochs at ${\sim}$1.0) yields 3-seed mean PPL $17.657 \pm 0.006$ vs.\ $17.674 \pm 0.007$ for adaptive $\bstar$ ($\Delta{=}0.017$); the bulk of D\&R's full-length advantage (0.384 PPL; D\&R full is seed\,42 only) is attributable to multi-epoch exposure (Table~\ref{tab:epoch_match}).
D\&R also demands threshold calibration: raw PPL traces a U-shaped curve ($q{>}0.1$: 17.40, $q{>}0.3$: 17.25, $q{>}0.9$: 17.42), suggesting an optimal threshold near $q{>}0.3$.
However, epoch-matched comparisons eliminate the U-shape entirely, revealing monotonically decreasing PPL that saturates near the adaptive level at $q{\geq}0.5$ (Figure~\ref{fig:dr_dual_curve}, Appendix~\ref{app:hybrid}).
The apparent optimum at $q{>}0.3$ is not a genuine quality threshold; it is the point where multi-epoch exposure happens to compensate maximally for the information loss from filtering.
